pages.title: Chapter 1: What is the point of Rhetoric?
pages.description: Aristotle defines rhetoric as the counterpart of dialectic and argues that a systematic art of proof, not appeals to emotion, is its true business.

pages.title: Chapter 10: Litigation: accusation and defense
pages.description: The motives behind wrongdoing — chance, nature, compulsion, habit, reason, anger, and desire — as material for accusation and defense.

audience.guidance_text: Read this chapter for Aristotle's seven causes of human action, the foundation for arguing about motive in a case.

pages.title: Chapter 11: Motive
pages.description: Aristotle explains motive through what people find pleasant, laying the ground for why people commit wrongdoing.

audience.guidance_text: Ties the psychology of pleasure to motive, background for the wrongdoing chapters either side of it.

pages.title: Chapter 12: Intent
pages.description: The frame of mind of wrongdoers and the circumstances and victims that make wrongdoing seem safe to attempt.

audience.guidance_text: Read alongside Chapter 11 (Motive) for the full picture of why and when people commit wrong.

pages.title: Chapter 13: Justice and Legislation
pages.description: Aristotle classifies just and unjust acts under particular and general law, and defines equity.

audience.guidance_text: Introduces the equity concept this book leans on when arguing written law against natural justice.

pages.title: Chapter 14: Severity of transgressions
pages.description: How to argue that a wrong act is greater or lesser in degree, with the rhetorical grounds for each.

audience.guidance_text: A short, practical chapter on aggravating and mitigating arguments for use in the law courts.

pages.title: Chapter 15: Trial Proceedings
pages.description: The five inartificial proofs of forensic oratory — laws, witnesses, contracts, torture, and oaths.

audience.guidance_text: Closes Book I with the concrete evidentiary tools an orator argues from in court.

pages.title: Chapter 2: Argumentation techniques
pages.description: Rhetoric as the faculty of finding the available means of persuasion: moral character, emotion, and the argument itself, via example and enthymeme.

pages.title: Chapter 3: Types of Rhetoric
pages.description: The three kinds of rhetorical speech — deliberative, forensic, and epideictic — their proper times, and the distinct end each one argues toward.

pages.title: Chapter 4: Topics of deliberative rhetoric
pages.description: The five subjects the deliberative orator must be ready to advise on: ways and means, war and peace, defence, food supply, and legislation.

pages.title: Chapter 5: What people care about
pages.description: A working definition of happiness and its parts — birth, friends, wealth, honor, health, beauty, strength, and good fortune — for the deliberative orator.

pages.title: Chapter 6: The greater good, and its components
pages.description: Aristotle defines the good as what all things aim at, catalogs the things generally recognized as good, and lists arguments for doubtful goods.

audience.guidance_text: Read this chapter to see how Aristotle catalogs the things people take to be good — the raw material deliberative speeches argue from.

pages.title: Chapter 7: The Impact of actions and trade-offs
pages.description: How to weigh one good against another: Aristotle's rules for comparing things by size, cause, scarcity, duration, and general opinion.

audience.guidance_text: Read this chapter for Aristotle's method of comparing two goods when both sides agree they are useful but disagree on which is more so.

pages.title: Chapter 8: Types of Governments
pages.description: The four forms of government — democracy, oligarchy, aristocracy, monarchy — their ends, and why an orator must know them.

audience.guidance_text: Read this chapter to see why knowing your audience's form of government shapes what arguments will persuade them.

pages.title: Chapter 9: Epideictic Rhetoric, praise and blame, virtue and vice
pages.description: Aristotle defines virtue and the noble, then sets out the topics and amplification techniques used in epideictic praise and blame.

audience.guidance_text: Read this chapter for the building blocks of praise and blame — the raw material of epideictic rhetoric.
